meta.title: Cristo — Chronology
meta.subtitle: Chronology of Jesus of Nazareth as the sources date him, of the objects venerated as his relics, and of where those objects are kept today
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of Jesus of Nazareth — the dates the Gospels, the ancient historians and modern scholars give for his life; the first places built to remember it — and of the objects venerated as relics of his life and Passion: when each first appears in the record, what was done to and with it, what laboratories have found, and which church, museum or community keeps it today.
meta.dataQualityNote: Work-in-progress dataset compiled from public sources (see references). The life of Jesus is dated as the sources date it: the Gospels are cited as the texts that narrate it, the ancient historians and modern scholars for the dates they establish, and where they disagree — the year of the birth, the year and day of the crucifixion — the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved. Miracles and the Resurrection are recorded as what the Gospels narrate and the Church believes; the site neither asserts nor denies them. The relics are recorded object by object: each entry states one authority's act about one named object and cites the document. Expositions, feasts, indulgences, jubilees and papal visits are acts of cult, not rulings on authenticity, and no Church act declaring any of these objects authentic was located. Laboratory results belong to their laboratories; published critiques are recorded as critiques. Years before the common era are written BCE. Dates resting on a single source, or on a source that could not be read in full, are flagged with a ? mark. Corrections against primary sources are welcome.

threads.note: These lanes are an editorial reading of this chronology, not a neutral index. They separate what the Gospels narrate and scholars date, what non-Christian writers and the ground itself attest, and the history of the objects venerated as relics — so that a reader can see which kind of evidence stands behind each entry. They are not a ranking of that evidence: the lane an event sits in says what kind of source it rests on, not whether it is true. Left out on purpose: the history of doctrine and of the Church, which belong to other chronologies.

lanes.label: The life, as the sources date it
lanes.basis: The events of Jesus's life as the Gospels narrate them, placed in time by the anchors the texts themselves give (Herod, the census of Quirinius, the fifteenth year of Tiberius, Pontius Pilate) and by the date ranges of modern scholarship, each attributed.

lanes.label: Outside witnesses and memory-sites
lanes.basis: What non-Christian ancient writers (Josephus, Tacitus, Pliny, Suetonius) and archaeology say, and the first churches built on the places the Gospels name — each cited to the text, the object or its custodian.

lanes.label: The objects venerated as relics
lanes.basis: Each object's first attestation, custody, transfers, tests and the acts of Church authorities about it, one act about one object at a time (core ADR-0007, applied to relics).

facts.label: Shroud of Turin
facts.value: Turin Cathedral, Italy, sealed and normally not visible. Owned by the Holy See since 1983; kept by the Archbishop of Turin as Pontifical Custodian. Radiocarbon-dated in 1988 to 1260–1390, a result contested by later critiques; the custodian says the tradition "cannot yet be said to be definitively proven".

facts.label: Sudarium of Oviedo
facts.value: Cámara Santa of Oviedo Cathedral, Spain. First attested in 1075. Radiocarbon results are reported for 1990–1992 and 2007, but no primary publication of them was located.

facts.label: Veil of Veronica and the Volto Santo
facts.value: St Peter's Basilica, Vatican City, exposed each fifth Sunday of Lent; and the Capuchin shrine of Manoppello, Italy, which claims the original Veronica for itself. The two claims conflict.

facts.label: Holy Tunic
facts.value: Trier Cathedral, Germany (first attested 1196; not visible, its authenticity "cannot be answered with certainty", per the cathedral); and the Basilica of Saint-Denys, Argenteuil, France (first attested 1156; radiocarbon-dated to 530–650, per the parish, which last exposed it in April–May 2025).

facts.label: Holy Blood
facts.value: Basilica of the Holy Blood, Bruges, Belgium, venerated daily; the procession is on UNESCO's intangible-heritage list. The basilica records that historians strongly doubt the traditional arrival in 1150.

facts.label: True Cross
facts.value: Fragments at Santa Croce in Gerusalemme (Rome; relic chapel closed from April 2026), St Peter's, Notre-Dame de Paris, the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem and the Mother See of Etchmiadzin, among many others. First attested c. 348–350; no scientific dating of the wood was located.

facts.label: Titulus Crucis
facts.value: Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Rome. Found in 1492; radiocarbon-dated in 2002 to AD 980–1146.

facts.label: Holy Nails
facts.value: Santa Croce (Rome), Notre-Dame de Paris, the Iron Crown of Monza and the pin of Vienna's Holy Lance, among some thirty venerated nails; the Catholic Encyclopedia holds that "very little reliance" can be placed on most.

facts.label: Crown of Thorns
facts.value: Notre-Dame de Paris, since its return on 13 December 2024; shown every Friday and venerated on the first Friday of the month. In Paris since 1239.

facts.label: Holy Lances
facts.value: At least four objects: St Peter's, Vatican City (received 1492); the Imperial Treasury, Vienna (an 8th-century lance, per its museum); Etchmiadzin, Armenia; and Kraków. Which, if any, is the lance "found" at Antioch in 1098 is disputed.

facts.label: Scala Sancta
facts.value: Pontifical Sanctuary of the Scala Santa, Rome, kept by the Passionists; venerated as the stairs of Pilate's palace by a tradition the sanctuary reports as tradition.

facts.label: Columns of the Flagellation
facts.value: Two rival claims: a black-and-white column at Santa Prassede, Rome, and a red porphyry fragment in the Franciscan chapel of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem. Different stones. The Custody's own pages date the Jerusalem fragment's arrival at the Holy Sepulchre differently: 1553 and the 14th century.

facts.label: Holy Chalice
facts.value: Valencia Cathedral, Spain: an agate cup the cathedral dates to the 1st century BC, with medieval mounts, venerated by tradition as the cup of the Last Supper. Since 2015 the Apostolic Penitentiary has made it a perpetual jubilee site — an act of cult. Genoa's Sacro Catino, once called the Grail, was shown in 1806 to be glass.

facts.label: What the Church has decided about authenticity
facts.value: No Church act declaring any of these objects authentic was located. John Paul II said in 1998 that the Church "has no specific competence to pronounce" on the Shroud; the Holy See's 2017 instruction on relics concerns relics of the Blessed and the Saints. Expositions, feasts, indulgences and papal visits are acts of cult, recorded as such.

events.dateNote: The Catechetical Lectures are dated c. 348–350.
events.title: Cyril of Jerusalem: the wood of the Cross is already distributed
events.text: In his Catechetical Lectures, Bishop Cyril of Jerusalem says that "the whole world has since been filled with pieces of the wood of the Cross", taken from Jerusalem by the faithful — the earliest attestation of Cross relics this project located. Cyril does not name Helena.

events.title: Egeria sees the wood and the title venerated on Good Friday
events.text: The pilgrim Egeria describes a silver-gilt casket brought out at Golgotha on Good Friday, from which "both the wood of the Cross and the title" are placed on a table and guarded by deacons, because someone had once bitten off a piece.

events.dateNote: Delivered on 25 February 395, per the Judaism and Rome commentary.
events.title: Ambrose credits Helena with finding the Cross
events.text: In his funeral oration for Theodosius, Ambrose of Milan narrates that Helena found three crosses and identified Christ's by its title, and that she found the nails — the first account this project located that connects Helena with the finding. Eusebius, writing earlier about her journey, does not; later writers such as Rufinus say the Cross was recognised by a miracle, not by the title.

events.dateNote: The Custody of the Holy Land and the Catholic Encyclopedia's "Jerusalem" give 614; the same encyclopedia's "Holy Lance" gives 615.
events.title: The Persians take the relic of the Cross from Jerusalem
events.text: Persian forces capture Jerusalem and carry off the relic of the Cross, per the Custody of the Holy Land and the Catholic Encyclopedia.

events.dateNote: The Custody of the Holy Land gives 630; the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 629.
events.title: Heraclius restores the Cross to Jerusalem
events.text: The Byzantine emperor Heraclius brings the relic back to Jerusalem. The Catholic Encyclopedia links the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) to his return — a feast, an act of cult.

events.dateNote: 13 March 1075 per Oviedo Cathedral; secondary accounts give 14 March. The record of the opening itself was not read.
events.title: The Arca Santa of Oviedo is opened: the Sudarium enters the record
events.text: At the solemn opening of the Arca Santa before King Alfonso VI, the relics listed include "de sudario Domini", per the cathedral — the first unambiguous attestation of the cloth now called the Sudarium of Oviedo. The cathedral's account of the ark's journey from Jerusalem in 614 is its tradition.

events.dateNote: June 1098, during the siege of Antioch; the day was not established.
events.title: A lance is "found" at Antioch
events.text: During the First Crusade, the Provençal pilgrim Peter Bartholomew reports visions of the apostle Andrew and leads a dig that produces a lance, per the chronicler Raymond d'Aguiliers. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls it a "discovery under very questionable circumstances"; which, if any, of the surviving lances it was is disputed.

events.title: The Sacro Catino reaches Genoa
events.text: Guglielmo Embriaco brings to Genoa a green hexagonal dish long held to be emerald and later called the Holy Grail, per the Italian Ministry of Culture. In 1806 it was established to be glass.

events.title: The Argenteuil tunic is first attested
events.text: A charter records an exposition of the tunic at Argenteuil organised by the Archbishop of Rouen in the presence of Louis VII — the first attestation, per the custodian parish, whose tradition dates the tunic's arrival to Charlemagne's time.

events.title: The crusaders' relic of the Cross is lost at Hattin
events.text: At the battle of Hattin the crusader army carries its relic of the Cross and loses it: "The Holy Cross also was lost," one contemporary account records; another reports a Templar's claim to have buried it, and a search that found nothing.

events.title: The Holy Tunic of Trier is first attested
events.text: Archbishop Johann I encloses the tunic in the new high altar of Trier Cathedral, per the Gesta Treverorum as the diocese reports it. The diocese itself describes the story of Helena sending the tunic to Trier as a legend: "a historical event was invented to explain a state of affairs".

events.title: Louis IX brings the Crown of Thorns to Paris
events.text: Having redeemed the Crown from the Venetian bankers to whom the Latin emperors of Constantinople had pledged it, Louis IX receives it at Villeneuve-l'Archevêque on 10 August and carries it barefoot into Paris on 19 August, per the Diocese of Paris.

events.title: The Sainte-Chapelle is consecrated to house the Crown
events.text: The royal chapel Louis IX built for the Crown and his other Passion relics is consecrated. The Crown stays there until the Revolution; the Sainte-Chapelle does not hold it today.

events.title: The Holy Blood procession is first mentioned
events.text: A by-law of the Bruges porters' guild contains the oldest mention of the procession, per the Basilica of the Holy Blood — which also records that most historians strongly doubt the story of the relic's arrival in 1150 and trace the oldest reliable sources to the 13th century.

events.dateNote: The Catholic Encyclopedia's "Troyes" dates the founding of the Lirey church to 20 June 1353; its "Holy Shroud" says "we first hear of it about the year 1360". The documentary start of the cloth is dated c. 1353–1360.
events.title: The Shroud appears at Lirey
events.text: The knight Geoffroi de Charny founds a collegiate church at Lirey in which a cloth bearing the double image of a man is shown for veneration — the first unambiguous appearance of the object now kept in Turin.

events.dateNote: c. 1389. The memorandum survives as an unsigned, undated draft; whether it was sent is disputed.
events.title: Bishop Pierre d'Arcis: the Lirey cloth is "cunningly painted"
events.text: In a memorandum to the Avignon pope Clement VII, the Bishop of Troyes writes that an earlier inquiry by his predecessor had found the cloth "cunningly painted, the truth being attested by the artist who had painted it". The memorandum is his account; defenders of the Shroud dispute its status.

events.dateNote: The bulls themselves were not read; both readings below are the Catholic Encyclopedia's, in two different articles.
events.title: Clement VII rules on the Lirey expositions — read two ways
events.text: The Avignon pope issues bulls on the Lirey cloth. The Catholic Encyclopedia's "Troyes" says they "approved the exposition as lawful"; its "Holy Shroud" says the pope required the priest to "declare in a loud voice that it was not the real shroud of Christ, but only a picture made to represent it". Either way the act regulates exposition; it is not a ruling that the cloth is authentic.

events.title: The Titulus Crucis is found at Santa Croce
events.text: During works at Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, a lead box is found bearing the inscription "HIC EST TITULUS VERAE CRUCIS", per the diarist Stefano Infessura; three other contemporaries give differing versions of where and how. A Leiden medievalist reads the timing as tied to the fall of Granada; the basilica calls the tablet a relic "probably" brought there in the 6th century.

events.title: Sultan Bayezid II sends a lance to Innocent VIII
events.text: A lance kept in Constantinople is given to Pope Innocent VIII by the Ottoman sultan, per Vatican News; it is still exposed in St Peter's in Lent. The Catholic Encyclopedia records that "great doubts as to its authenticity were felt at Rome" at the time, because of rival lances.

events.dateNote: The year is the custodian's; the day was not verified.
events.title: The Shroud is damaged by fire at Chambéry
events.text: A fire in the Savoy chapel at Chambéry leaves the burn lines and holes still visible on the cloth, per the custodian archdiocese.

events.title: Calvin's Treatise on Relics
events.text: Jean Calvin argues that the pieces of the Cross shown across Europe would fill "a good big ship" though the Gospel says one man could carry it — the classic Protestant case against the relics, answered in 1870 by Rohault de Fleury.

events.title: The Shroud is moved to Turin
events.text: The Dukes of Savoy move the cloth from Chambéry to Turin — to shorten the pilgrimage of Archbishop Carlo Borromeo of Milan, per the custodian archdiocese.

events.title: Borromeo establishes the cult of the Holy Nail at Monza
events.text: Archbishop Carlo Borromeo establishes the cult of the Sacred Nail "to make official the recognition of the diadem as a relic", per the Monza cathedral museum — an act of cult about the Iron Crown's inner band. The same museum reports recent studies dating the crown to between the 4th–5th and the 9th centuries.

events.title: Sixtus V moves the Scala Sancta
events.text: The stairs venerated as those of Pilate's palace are moved to their present site beside the Lateran. The tradition that Helena brought them to Rome is attributed by the Catholic Encyclopedia to "the historians of the monument".

events.title: The Crown of Thorns is assigned to Notre-Dame
events.text: After the Revolution moved it to Saint-Denis and the national library, the Crown is handed to the Archbishop of Paris and placed in the treasury of Notre-Dame, per the Diocese of Paris.

events.title: Pius IX entrusts the Scala Sancta to the Passionists
events.text: By the constitution Decet Romanum Pontificem, and a second act of 1854, Pius IX gives the sanctuary's custody to the Passionist Fathers, per the sanctuary — acts about custody, not about the stairs' origin.

events.title: Rohault de Fleury measures the relics of the Cross
events.text: Answering Calvin, the antiquarian Charles Rohault de Fleury estimates the known Cross relics at about 5 million cubic millimetres and argues that, even tripled for relics unknown, they make under a tenth of the 180 million he computes for a cross. The Catholic Encyclopedia later restates his figures slightly differently; neither calculation is established fact.

events.dateNote: The exposition ran from 25 May to 2 June 1898; the photograph was taken during it.
events.title: Secondo Pia photographs the Shroud
events.text: During an exposition, the lawyer Secondo Pia, authorised by the House of Savoy, photographs the cloth for the first time; his negative shows a positive-looking image, per the custodian archdiocese.

events.title: STURP examines the Shroud
events.text: After the fourth-centenary exposition, 44 scholars — among them the American Shroud of Turin Research Project — examine the cloth for 120 hours, per the custodian. STURP's 1981 summary reports no pigments on the fibrils and a real human form; the microscopist Walter McCrone argued the image was paint. The disagreement is recorded, not resolved.

events.title: The Shroud passes to the Holy See
events.text: At the death of Umberto II of Savoy, the cloth passes by his bequest to the Holy See, which has owned it since; the Archbishop of Turin keeps it as Pontifical Custodian.

events.place: Tucson, Arizona, USA / Oxford, United Kingdom / Zurich, Switzerland
events.title: Radiocarbon dating places the Shroud's linen in 1260–1390
events.text: The Arizona, Oxford and Zurich laboratories report in Nature that "the age of the shroud is obtained as AD 1260-1390, with at least 95% confidence". Later critiques contest the sample and the statistics, among them a 2019 analysis of the raw data in Archaeometry; the result and the critiques are each their authors'.

events.title: Fire in Turin Cathedral; the Shroud is carried out undamaged
events.text: Fire destroys Guarini's chapel; the cloth, moved to the choir in 1993, is carried to safety and found to have suffered no damage, per the custodian.

events.title: John Paul II: the Church "has no specific competence to pronounce"
events.text: Visiting the exposition, John Paul II says: "Since it is not a matter of faith, the Church has no specific competence to pronounce on these questions. She entrusts to scientists the task of continuing to investigate". He calls the cloth "a mirror of the Gospel" — a devotional reading, not a verdict either way.

events.title: Radiocarbon dating places the Titulus in 980–1146
events.text: Physicists of Roma Tre University report in Radiocarbon that the walnut tablet dates to AD 980–1146 (two sigma), and note that this "permits one to consider" that it is a copy of an original. The result is the laboratory's.

events.title: The Argenteuil tunic is radiocarbon-dated to 530–650
events.text: A dating by the French CEA laboratory at Saclay gives "between the years 530 and 650", per the custodian parish, which reports the researchers' warning about contamination and maintains its case for authenticity. A 2005 test on another fragment, commissioned privately, gave 670–880 and is contested.

events.dateNote: The sleeves were removed in February 2004 for the study of 2003–2004.
events.title: Vienna's Holy Lance is dated to the 8th century
events.text: A University of Vienna study, with the gold and silver sleeves removed for the first time since 1924, finds a winged lance of a form "typical of the second half of the 8th century". The Kunsthistorisches Museum, which keeps it, writes that its central pin later came to be venerated as a Nail and the lance, in the 13th century, as that of Longinus.

events.title: Benedict XVI visits the Volto Santo of Manoppello
events.text: The pope makes what the text calls a private pilgrimage to the Capuchin shrine, speaking of the Holy Face; the address does not use the words "veil" or "relic". The shrine identifies its image with the Veronica, which St Peter's still exposes as its own.

events.title: Benedict XVI calls the Shroud "the Icon of Holy Saturday"
events.text: At the 2010 exposition the pope describes the cloth as "an Icon written in blood" — a devotional reading, recorded as an act of cult.

events.dateNote: The pilgrimage ran from 13 April to 13 May 2012.
events.title: The Holy Tunic is shown at Trier
events.text: The most recent Trier pilgrimage. The cathedral, which keeps the tunic out of sight in a climate-controlled case, states that "the question of the Holy Robe's authenticity cannot be answered with certainty".

events.title: The marble of the Scala Sancta is uncovered
events.text: After restoration, the 28 steps are shown without their wooden covering for 60 days, "for the first time after almost 300 years", per the Vatican Museums.

events.title: The Crown of Thorns is rescued from the Notre-Dame fire
events.text: As Notre-Dame burns, the Crown is carried out; the fire brigade's chaplain, Jean-Marc Fournier, has described his part on air, and reports credit a chain of firefighters and police.

events.title: A fragment of the Holy Crib is sent to Bethlehem
events.text: At Pope Francis's wish a fragment of the wooden slats kept at Santa Maria Maggiore is taken for the Franciscans of Bethlehem, per Vatican News — a gift and an act of cult. The basilica says the slats were "scientifically" dated to the time of Christ's birth but cites no study.

events.title: The Crown of Thorns returns to Notre-Dame
events.text: Six days after the cathedral reopens, Archbishop Laurent Ulrich presides over the Crown's return to Notre-Dame, where it now rests in a new reliquary, per the Diocese of Paris.

events.title: The Custodian declines to rule on new Shroud hypotheses
events.text: Answering claims published in 2025, the Pontifical Custodian, Cardinal Roberto Repole, states that he "has no reason to enter into the merits of hypotheses freely put forward by scientists".

events.title: St Peter's exposes the Veronica
events.text: The annual Rite of the Holy Face on the fifth Sunday of Lent shows the veil from the Veronica loggia as "the Major Relic of the Holy Face" — an act of cult.

events.title: Santa Croce's relic chapel closes for urgent works
events.text: The basilica announces that its Chapel of the Relics — which holds the Cross fragments, the Titulus and a Nail — is temporarily closed by order of the Vicariate of Rome and the Ministry of Culture.

figures.name: Helena
figures.role: Mother of Constantine; journeyed to Palestine after 324 and built churches there, per the Catholic Encyclopedia citing Eusebius. The finding of the Cross is first credited to her by Ambrose in 395

figures.name: Louis IX
figures.role: King of France; acquired the Crown of Thorns in 1239 and built the Sainte-Chapelle to house it

figures.name: Heraclius
figures.role: Byzantine emperor; returned the relic of the Cross to Jerusalem in 629 or 630

figures.name: Geoffroi de Charny
figures.role: Knight and lord of Lirey, in whose collegiate church the cloth now in Turin was first shown

figures.name: Pierre d'Arcis
figures.role: Bishop of Troyes; his memorandum of c. 1389 reports an earlier finding that the Lirey cloth was painted

figures.name: Secondo Pia
figures.role: Lawyer and photographer; took the first photograph of the Shroud in 1898

figures.name: Peter Bartholomew
figures.role: Provençal pilgrim of the First Crusade who led the Antioch lance "discovery" of 1098

figures.name: Jean Calvin
figures.role: Reformer; his Treatise on Relics (1543) is the classic Protestant critique of the Passion relics

organizations.name: Archdiocese of Turin — Pontifical Custodian of the Shroud
organizations.relation: Keeps the Shroud for its owner, the Holy See; the Custodian is the Archbishop of Turin

organizations.name: Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme
organizations.relation: Keeps Cross fragments, the Titulus and a Nail

organizations.name: Archdiocese of Paris and the chapter of Notre-Dame
organizations.relation: Keeps the Crown of Thorns, a Cross fragment and a Nail, under the statutory guard of the Order of the Holy Sepulchre

organizations.name: Custody of the Holy Land
organizations.relation: The Franciscan province that keeps the Latin relics at the Holy Sepulchre and the Crib fragment at Bethlehem

organizations.name: Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien — Imperial Treasury
organizations.relation: A state museum that keeps the Vienna Holy Lance and publishes its dating

organizations.name: Centro Español de Sindonología
organizations.relation: An association that studies the Sudarium and argues for its compatibility with the Shroud — an interested party, not a custodian

disambiguation.note: This subject is contested terrain twice over: between faith and historical criticism about the life, and between tradition and the laboratory about the relics. These distinctions are the ones readers most often flatten.

items.title: Shroud ≠ Sudarium
items.text: The Shroud of Turin is a full-length linen bearing the double image of a man; the Sudarium of Oviedo is a face cloth with stains and no image. They are different objects in different cities; the claim that they fit together is that of the Spanish sindonologists, not a finding.

items.title: Veronica ≠ Manoppello ≠ Mandylion
items.text: Three objects, three legends: the Veronica is the veil of the Way of the Cross kept at St Peter's; the Volto Santo of Manoppello is an image its Capuchin shrine identifies with the lost original, which St Peter's does not concede; the Mandylion is the image the Abgar legend ties to Edessa.

items.title: Titulus ≠ True Cross
items.text: The Titulus is a separate object with a separate history: first recorded in Rome in 1492 and radiocarbon-dated to 980–1146. No dating of the Cross wood was located.

items.title: Several Holy Lances
items.text: The lances of St Peter's, Vienna, Etchmiadzin and Kraków are separate objects with separate histories; the lance "found" at Antioch in 1098 is identified with more than one of them by different authors.

items.title: An act of cult is not a verdict of authenticity
items.text: Expositions, feasts, indulgences, jubilees, basilicas and papal visits honour or regulate veneration; they are not rulings that an object is what tradition says. The Holy See's 2017 instruction on relics concerns relics of the Blessed and the Saints. This site records each act about each object as what it is.

items.title: A laboratory date is its laboratory's
items.text: Radiocarbon and other test results are recorded with their authors and journals, and published critiques as critiques. A date range dates the sample tested, not the tradition attached to the object.

placesMap.note: Every recorded event that names a place is placed here — the places of the life as the Gospels and scholars locate them, and the churches, museums and treasuries where the relics were first recorded, moved and kept. An event that names two places is drawn at both. The year control is an aid, not a claim: several dates here are ranges or disputed, and a slider cannot show a disagreement, so read the dashed markers and the chronology entries for what is settled.
